node.label: Charles Tilly
node.date_label: 1964 The Vendée · 1985 War Making and State Making as Organized Crime · 1986 The Contentious French
node.description: Charles Tilly combined historical sociology with research on collective action, revolution and state formation. His studies range from counterrevolution in the Vendée to changing French political repertoires and comparisons across European states. In his essay on war making, coercion and extraction help explain the growth of state organizations, while resistance and bargaining constrain rulers. These are historically situated arguments; he explicitly rejects treating early modern Europe as a ready-made forecast for twentieth-century societies.

proposed_edges.relationship: War finance and organized coercion help shape European state formation
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary chapter 169–172 links warfare, resource extraction and capital accumulation; analogy with protection rackets is an argument, not a claim that every state is identical to a criminal organization.

proposed_edges.relationship: Coercion and bargaining are analysed as historically variable processes
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary chapter 169–170 says popular resistance could force rulers to concede protection and constraints, and rejects direct future-from-European-past extrapolation. This scoped mechanism claim supplies no universal historical sequence.
